lines.text: Three thousand years of conflict, from chariots on the Orontes to drones over Ukraine. These are the wars that drew the borders and shaped the world we live in.
Our story begins in Syria, in 1274 BCE, where the chariots of Ramesses the Second met the Hittite army. It is one of the first battles whose tactics we truly know.
Around 500 BCE, a Chinese book on strategy, credited to Sun Tzu, taught that the finest victory is the one won without fighting at all.
Soon the Persian Empire turned on the Greeks. At Marathon and at Salamis the small city-states held, and mainland Greece stayed free.
Then the Greeks turned on each other. For almost thirty years Athens fought Sparta, and Athens lost, a war recorded by the historian Thucydides.
In barely eleven years, a young Macedonian king, Alexander, conquered the whole Persian Empire and marched his army all the way to India.
In the west, Rome and Carthage fought three great wars for the Mediterranean. They ended in 146 BCE with Carthage destroyed.
Carthage's greatest general, Hannibal, crossed the Alps with elephants and crushed Rome at Cannae, but he was finally beaten at Zama.
Far to the east, the state of Qin conquered its six rivals one by one, and in 221 BCE China was united for the first time.
Julius Caesar spent seven years bringing Gaul, roughly today's France and Belgium, under Roman rule, and wrote his own account of the campaign.
Within a century of Muhammad, Arab armies carried the rule of the caliphate from Arabia to Spain in the west and Central Asia in the east.
From the end of the eleventh century, Christian armies from Europe set out to take and hold Jerusalem. The Crusades went on for about two hundred years.
Then came the Mongols. Genghis Khan and his heirs built the largest connected land empire in history, stretching from Korea toward Europe.
England and France fought on and off for more than a century over the French crown, through Crecy, Agincourt and the rise of Joan of Arc.
In 1453 the cannon of Mehmed the Second broke the walls of Constantinople. After about two months of siege, the Byzantine Empire was gone.
In Mexico, Hernan Cortes and a small Spanish force, helped by many Indigenous allies and by disease, brought down the Aztec Empire within two years.
In the 1590s Japan twice invaded Korea, hoping to go on to China. Korea, aided by Ming China and the brilliant Admiral Yi, drove them out.
In Europe, a quarrel over religion grew into the Thirty Years War, a struggle for power that devastated the German lands until the Peace of Westphalia.
In England, king and Parliament went to war over who held power. In 1649 King Charles the First was tried and executed.
By the 1750s the wars of Europe spanned the globe. In the Seven Years War, Britain and France fought for empire in Europe, America and India.
Soon after, thirteen British colonies in North America rose up. With help from France, they won their independence as the United States.
Then Napoleon took France to war against coalition after coalition. For a decade he redrew the map of Europe.
While Spain was weakened, its colonies in the Americas broke away, led by figures such as Simon Bolivar, until most of the continent was free.
Napoleon's final battle came in 1815 at Waterloo, in today's Belgium, where Wellington and the Prussians ended his rule for good.
In 1839 Britain went to war with China when the Qing banned the opium trade. China lost, and Hong Kong passed into British hands.
China was soon torn apart from within. The Taiping Rebellion, led by a man who called himself the brother of Jesus, became one of the deadliest wars ever fought.
In the Crimean War, Russia faced the Ottomans, Britain and France. New weapons and disease made it a grim lesson in modern warfare.
Born in 1856, Woodrow Wilson would one day lead America into the First World War and dream of a League of Nations to end such wars.
In 1857 Indian soldiers at Meerut rose against the East India Company, and revolt spread across the north. Afterward, Britain ruled India directly.
Meanwhile in Germany, the future Kaiser Wilhelm the Second was born. He would build a great navy and lead his country into world war.
In 1861 the United States split in two over slavery. Four years of civil war ended with the Union preserved and slavery abolished.
Its turning point came at Gettysburg, in Pennsylvania, where over three days the Union army threw back Robert E. Lee's invasion of the North.
In 1870 Prussia crushed France and captured its emperor. Out of victory, a new German Empire was proclaimed.
Born in 1874, Winston Churchill would become Britain's wartime prime minister, whose speeches held the country together in its darkest hour.
Joseph Stalin, born in Georgia in 1878, would rule the Soviet Union through terror and lead it to victory over Nazi Germany.
Douglas MacArthur, born in 1880, would command in the Pacific, oversee the occupation of Japan and later lead the UN forces in Korea.
From the 1880s, European powers carved up Africa by treaty and by force. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
Franklin Roosevelt, born in 1882, would be elected president four times and lead America through most of the Second World War.
A year later came Benito Mussolini, who would found Fascism, rule Italy as dictator and tie his country's fate to Hitler.
Hideki Tojo, born in 1884, would be Japan's prime minister when it struck Pearl Harbor, and was later tried and hanged for war crimes.
Bernard Montgomery, born in 1887, would win the battle of El Alamein in the Egyptian desert and command Allied ground forces in Normandy.
In 1889 Adolf Hitler was born in Austria. As dictator of Germany, he would start the Second World War and order the Holocaust.
Dwight Eisenhower, born in 1890, would plan the D-Day landings as Supreme Allied Commander, and later become president.
That same year came Charles de Gaulle, who would lead the Free French from London and later found France's Fifth Republic.
Erwin Rommel, the Desert Fox, would lead the Afrika Korps in North Africa before being forced to take his own life.
Mao Zedong, born in 1893, would win China's civil war and found the People's Republic, with campaigns that cost millions of lives.
Nikita Khrushchev, born in 1894, would denounce Stalin and stand at the brink with America during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
Georgy Zhukov, born in 1896, would defend Moscow, win at Stalingrad and Kursk, and lead the Red Army all the way to Berlin.
At the turn of the century, Britain fought the two Boer republics of southern Africa, and won only after a long and bitter guerrilla war.
In 1901 Hirohito was born, the emperor who would reign over Japan's war and announce its surrender to his people in 1945.
In 1905 Japan stunned the world by defeating Russia, sinking its fleet at Tsushima. An Asian power had beaten a European empire.
Leonid Brezhnev, born in 1906, would lead the Soviet Union through a thaw with the West, and into the invasion of Afghanistan.
Ronald Reagan, born in 1911, would go from Hollywood to the White House, build up America's military and meet Gorbachev to cut nuclear arms.
A year later came Kim Il Sung, who would found North Korea and launch the Korean War in 1950.
On the twenty-eighth of June 1914, the heir to Austria-Hungary was shot dead in Sarajevo. Within weeks, Europe was at war.
The Great War pulled in empires across the world. Millions died, and by its end four empires had fallen.
In the east, in August 1914, German forces surrounded and destroyed a Russian army at Tannenberg.
In the west, the French and British stopped the German advance on the Marne, just short of Paris. Hopes of a quick war died, and the trenches began.
In 1915 the Allies tried to force the Dardanelles and knock the Ottomans out of the war. After months of slaughter at Gallipoli, they withdrew.
That spring, a German submarine sank the liner Lusitania off Ireland. The loss of so many civilians, Americans among them, turned opinion against Germany.
To break the deadlock came a new machine: the tank, an armoured vehicle on tracks, built to roll over trenches and barbed wire.
And a new horror: poison gas, released on the Western Front. Today such weapons are banned by international treaty.
In 1916 Germany attacked the French fortress of Verdun, and France held it for most of the year at an enormous cost on both sides.
At sea, the British and German fleets met off Jutland in the war's greatest naval battle. Britain lost more ships but kept control of the sea.
On the Somme, Britain suffered its worst single day of losses ever, and months of fighting gained only a few miles.
In 1917 John F. Kennedy was born, the president who would face down the Soviet Union over missiles in Cuba.
That same year, revolution swept Russia. The tsar fell, and then Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power.
In Belgium, the British attacked at Passchendaele, through rain and deep mud. It became a byword for the suffering of the war.
In northern Italy, Austrian and German troops broke through at Caporetto, and the Italian army fell back a long way.
Inside Russia, the Bolshevik Red Army fought the Whites in a brutal civil war. The Reds won, and the Soviet Union was born.
As the war ended, an influenza pandemic swept the world, infecting a huge share of humanity and killing even more than the fighting had.
In Germany, sailors mutinied and revolt spread. The Kaiser gave up his throne, and a republic was declared.
Earlier that year, Soviet Russia had made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk, giving up vast lands to leave the war.
At eleven in the morning on the eleventh of November 1918, the guns fell silent on the Western Front. The armistice is still remembered every year.
At Versailles, the victors made Germany give up land, shrink its army and accept blame for the war, grievances that would not be forgotten.
To keep the peace, the League of Nations was founded in Geneva. It settled some disputes, but could not stop the aggression to come.
In 1922 the Soviet Union was formed, a communist state of many republics that would become one of the world's two superpowers.
Fidel Castro, born in 1926, would lead a revolution in Cuba and bind his island to the Soviet Union, ninety miles from America.
In China, Nationalists and Communists began a long civil war. It paused for the war with Japan, and ended with Communist victory in 1949.
France, meanwhile, built the Maginot Line, a chain of forts along its border with Germany. In 1940 the Germans simply went around it.
Mikhail Gorbachev, born in 1931, would open up the Soviet Union and agree to cut arms with the West, and then watch it come apart.
In Soviet Ukraine, forced collectivisation and grain seizures brought a terrible famine that killed millions. Many countries call it a genocide.
In 1933 Hitler took power and built Nazi Germany, a one-party dictatorship that would start a world war and carry out the Holocaust.
In Britain, a new fighter took to the air in 1936, the Spitfire, with its graceful elliptical wings. Its moment would come soon.
That year Spain fell into civil war. Germany and Italy backed Franco's Nationalists, the Soviet Union and foreign volunteers the Republic, and Franco won.
In the Soviet Union, Stalin's Great Purge had hundreds of thousands shot and many more sent to the Gulag camps.
In 1937 Japan launched a full war on China. It would last eight years, merge into the world war and kill millions of Chinese.
At Munich in 1938, Britain and France let Hitler take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia, hoping to buy peace. It did not.
That November, on Kristallnacht, synagogues and Jewish shops across Germany and Austria were smashed and burned, and many Jews were sent to camps.
In 1939 the United States began the secret work, with Britain and Canada, that would become the Manhattan Project and build the atomic bomb.
Germany launched its largest warship, the Bismarck. In 1941 she sank the Hood, and was hunted down and sunk only days later.
In September 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and the Second World War began, the largest and deadliest war in history.
In occupied Poland the Nazis built Auschwitz, where more than a million people, most of them Jews, were murdered.
In the summer of 1940 the Luftwaffe tried to win the skies over England. The Royal Air Force held, and the invasion of Britain never came.
Instead, German bombers struck British cities night after night, above all London. Tens of thousands died, but Britain did not give in.
In June 1941 Hitler turned east and invaded the Soviet Union, the largest land attack in history. Most of the war's fighting and dying would happen here.
Behind the front, Nazi Germany set out to murder the Jews of Europe. About six million were killed in the Holocaust, along with Roma and many others.
On the seventh of December 1941, Japan struck the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, and the United States entered the war.
Six months later, at Midway, American planes sank four Japanese carriers, and the tide turned in the Pacific.
On the Volga, Germany fought for months to take Stalingrad. The Red Army surrounded and captured the German Sixth Army, a turning point of the war.
In the Egyptian desert, Montgomery's Eighth Army broke the German and Italian forces at El Alamein, ending the threat to the Suez Canal.
In the spring of 1943 the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto took up arms against deportation to the death camps. They were crushed, but their courage is remembered.
That July, at Kursk, Germany launched its last great attack in the east in the largest tank battle of the war. The Soviets held, and pushed west.
On the sixth of June 1944, Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy, the largest seaborne invasion ever, and the liberation of France began.
Germany answered with the V-2, the first long-range ballistic missile, fired at London and Antwerp. Its designers would later help launch the space age.
That winter Germany made one last gamble in the west, through the Ardennes. It surprised the Allies, then ran out of fuel and was beaten back.
In February 1945 Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met at Yalta in Crimea to plan the end of the war and the shape of Europe after it.
In the Pacific, American Marines fought for weeks to take the island of Iwo Jima. Almost all its Japanese defenders died.
Then came Okinawa, the last great battle of the Pacific War, with terrible losses on both sides and among the island's people.
In Europe, the Red Army surrounded Berlin. Hitler died by his own hand in the ruins, and days later Germany surrendered.
But as one war ended another began, a cold one, between the United States and the Soviet Union, fought with arms races, spies and proxy wars.
At Potsdam that July, the Allied leaders agreed how to occupy Germany and called on Japan to surrender.
In August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing about a hundred thousand people at once. Japan surrendered.
That same year the United Nations was founded, so that the world might settle its quarrels without another war.
At Nuremberg, Allied judges tried the leaders of Nazi Germany for war crimes and crimes against humanity, laying a foundation for international law.
In Tokyo, a similar tribunal tried the leaders of wartime Japan. Several were sentenced to death.
In 1947 the diary of Anne Frank, a girl who hid from the Nazis in Amsterdam and did not survive, was published. It gave the Holocaust a human voice.
That August, British India was divided into India and Pakistan. Millions crossed the new borders, and terrible violence followed.
America's Marshall Plan sent billions of dollars to rebuild western Europe, to keep hunger and unrest at bay and bind Europe to the West.
In 1948 the State of Israel was declared and its Arab neighbours attacked. Israel survived, and about seven hundred thousand Palestinians lost their homes.
The Soviets cut the roads and railways to West Berlin. For almost a year the Western Allies fed the city by air.
In 1949 North America and western Europe formed NATO, promising that an attack on one would be an attack on all.
A year later, North Korea invaded the South. America and its UN allies fought China and the North, and the war ended in a divided peninsula.
In 1952 America tested the first hydrogen bomb, far more powerful than the bombs of 1945. The arms race had entered a new age.
That year Vladimir Putin was born, the intelligence officer who would lead Russia from 1999 and take it back to war in Europe.
In Cuba, Fidel Castro and Che Guevara began a guerrilla war, and in 1959 they overthrew the dictator Batista.
In 1954 Algerian nationalists rose against France. Eight years of war ended with Algeria's independence.
The Soviet Union answered NATO with the Warsaw Pact, an alliance that also kept its own eastern bloc in line.
In Vietnam, the communist North fought the American-backed South for twenty years. The war ended in 1975 with the fall of Saigon.
In 1956 Hungarians rose against their Soviet-backed rulers. Within weeks, Soviet tanks crushed the revolt in Budapest.
That autumn Britain, France and Israel attacked Egypt over the Suez Canal, and were forced to withdraw. The old colonial powers had lost their reach.
In 1960 an American spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union and its pilot captured, wrecking a summit in Paris.
In 1961 CIA-backed Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs to overthrow Castro, and failed, pushing Cuba closer to Moscow.
That summer East Germany built a wall straight through Berlin, splitting families and stopping people from leaving the east.
In October 1962, America found Soviet missiles in Cuba. For thirteen days the world stood closer to nuclear war than ever before or since.
In June 1967 Israel fought Egypt, Jordan and Syria in six days, and took Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.
In 1968 Czechoslovakia tried socialism with a human face. In August, Warsaw Pact tanks rolled in and ended the Prague Spring.
In 1971 East Pakistan fought for its freedom, and after a bloody war, Bangladesh was born.
In Chile, the army overthrew the elected president Salvador Allende. General Pinochet ruled for years, and thousands were killed or vanished.
That October, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel. The war brought an oil crisis, and in time peace between Egypt and Israel.
In 1978 Volodymyr Zelenskyy was born, a comic actor who would become president and lead Ukraine through Russia's full invasion.
In 1979 Soviet troops entered Afghanistan to prop up its communist government. Ten years of war against foreign-backed rebels followed before they left.
In 1980 shipyard workers in Gdansk founded Solidarity, the first free trade union in the Soviet bloc, and began to loosen communism's grip on Poland.
That same year Iraq invaded Iran. Eight years of trench warfare and poison gas ended in a ceasefire, with the borders hardly changed.
In 1982 Argentina seized the Falkland Islands, and Britain sent a task force across the world to take them back within weeks.
In 1989 a wave of mostly peaceful revolutions swept Eastern Europe, and one communist government after another fell.
In Beijing, students filled Tiananmen Square to call for reform. The government declared martial law and sent in the army.
In Germany, the divided country began to come together, and on the third of October 1990 it became one again.
It had started on the ninth of November 1989, when East Germany opened its border and crowds began tearing down the Berlin Wall.
In Czechoslovakia, the Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in a few weeks without a shot, and the playwright Vaclav Havel became president.
In 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait. A US-led coalition drove it out, with a ground war that lasted only days.
As Yugoslavia broke apart, war returned to Europe, in Croatia, in Bosnia and in Kosovo, the deadliest fighting on the continent since 1945.
After a failed coup in August 1991, the Soviet republics broke away. On the twenty-sixth of December, the Soviet Union ceased to exist, and the Cold War was over.
In 1994, over about a hundred days, Rwandan extremists murdered hundreds of thousands of Tutsi and moderate Hutu while the world looked away.
The violence spilled into Congo, where a war drawing in many nations became Africa's world war, the deadliest conflict since 1945.
On the eleventh of September 2001, al-Qaeda hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. Nearly three thousand people died.
Weeks later America and its allies invaded Afghanistan and toppled the Taliban. Twenty years on, they left, and the Taliban returned.
In 2003 a US-led coalition invaded Iraq and removed Saddam Hussein, followed by years of insurgency and sectarian bloodshed.
In December 2010 protests broke out in Tunisia and spread across the Arab world. Leaders fell in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen.
In Syria, protests against Bashar al-Assad became a many-sided war that killed hundreds of thousands and drove millions from their homes.
In 2014 war came to Ukraine, as Russia took Crimea and backed fighting in the Donbas.
That spring Russian troops seized the Crimean peninsula, and Moscow declared it part of Russia, a move most of the world never recognised.
That same year the Islamic State seized much of Iraq and Syria. A long war against it took back its last land in 2019.
And Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, fell into a civil war that has gone on ever since.
From 2018 a new kind of war took hold, as America and China piled tariffs on each other's goods.
In February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the largest war in Europe since the Second World War.
In 2023 Sudan collapsed into war between its army and the Rapid Support Forces.
That October, after the Hamas attack of the seventh, war returned to Gaza.
In May 2025, after an attack in Kashmir, India and Pakistan exchanged missile and drone strikes in a brief but dangerous clash.
That June, in a war of twelve days, Israel and the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites, and Iran fired missiles at Israel.
And in 2025 the United States put tariffs on goods from almost every country, the highest in a century, and the trade wars spread.
From Kadesh to the present, the wars go on, and so does the hope of a lasting peace.
